summary.en: María Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela, sparking protests demanding elections and her continued presence, while the United States has deployed Space Force electromagnetic and electronic warfare systems against Venezuela and pressured Reliance to refine Venezuelan oil. CIA Director Ratcliffe visited Havana with a paramilitary operative linked to a past operation that killed 32 Cuban soldiers, and the Pentagon has barred DoD personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. actions involving Venezuela, leading to the DOJ arrest of a soldier who made $400,000 betting on Maduro's removal. A bomb blast near the Colombia-Venezuela border injured at least four police officers, and an explosive attack on the same border injured six, including four officers. 2 battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: María Corina Machado har returnert til Venezuela, og har utløst protester som krever valg og hennes fortsatte tilstedeværelse, mens USA har satt i drift elektromagnetiske og elektroniske krigssystemer fra Space Force mot Venezuela og presset Reliance til å raffinere venezuelansk olje. CIA-direktør Ratcliffe besøkte Havanna sammen med en paramilitær operativ knyttet til en tidligere operasjon som drepte 32 kubanske soldater, og Pentagon har forbudt DoD-personell å bruke ikke-offentlig informasjon til å spekulere i amerikanske handlinger som involverer Venezuela, noe som førte til at DOJ arresterte en soldat som tjente 400 000 dollar på å satse på at Maduro ble fjernet. En bombeeksplosjon nær grensen mellom Colombia og Venezuela såret minst fire politibetjenter, og et eksplosivangrep på samme grense såret seks, inkludert fire betjenter. To dødsfall knyttet til kamp ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
